html:
The Tupi were one of the largest groups of Indigenous peoples of Brazil, speakers of Tupi-Guarani languages, who by the time of European contact held most of the Atlantic coast. The map shows them in 800 and 900.

Their ancestors probably came from the Amazon basin. From about 2,900 years ago they spread south and east, reaching the coast and pushing other peoples inland. They lived in villages of large communal houses, grew manioc in forest clearings, fished and hunted. Wars between villages were frequent, and captives were sometimes killed and eaten in ritual, as the German Hans Staden described after being held by the Tupinambá in the 1550s.

The Portuguese arrived in 1500 and traded for brazilwood. Disease, slavery and war soon devastated the coastal Tupi. Jesuit priests such as José de Anchieta wrote a grammar of Tupi, and a common language based on it was spoken widely in colonial Brazil. Many Brazilian words and place names, and words like "jaguar", come from Tupi. Their southern relatives are the Guarani.
